The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). A **finite-mode regulator** in this item is a fixed
finite nonempty label set $J$ with $N:=|J|\ge1$, a fixed enumeration of $J$ by
$\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and the real coordinate vector
$q=(q_1,\ldots,q_N)\in\mathbb R^N$. The labels may name sites of a finite
lattice or finitely many modes; their geometry enters only through the chosen
polynomial below. No limit in $N$ is part of this definition.

Choose real coefficients $a_1,\ldots,a_N>0$, constants $c>0$ and $C_0\ge0$,
and a real polynomial $V\in\mathbb R[q_1,\ldots,q_N]$ such that
$$V(q)\ge c|q|^2-C_0\qquad(q\in\mathbb R^N).$$
Let $H_N:=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, with vectors identified up to almost
everywhere equality and inner product
$$\langle u,v\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb R^N}u(q)\overline{v(q)}\,dq,$$
linear in the first variable. Under Countable Choice this is a complex Hilbert
space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Let
$D_0:=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$, the smooth compactly supported
complex-valued functions. The associated **polynomial differential expression**
is the map
$$h_0:D_0\to H_N,\qquad h_0u:=-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2u+Vu.$$
It is well defined because each derivative of $u$ and the product $Vu$ are
smooth and compactly supported. Set $W:=V+C_0+1$, so
$W(q)\ge1+c|q|^2$. This definition specifies finite mathematical data and a
differential expression; it does not choose a self-adjoint operator domain or
assert a continuum or infinite-volume limit.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $N\ge1$, $a_1,\ldots,a_N>0$ and $c>0$. Let
$Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ be the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$
for the form inner product
$$a_{\mathrm{osc}}(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int (\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv} +\int (c|q|^2+2)u\overline v.$$
This is the space $Q$ of
[[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]] for $V(q)=c|q|^2$ and $C_0=0$.
For $\mathbf n=(n_1,\ldots,n_N)\in\mathbb N_0^N$, there is a smooth product
Hermite function $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ such that
$$\langle\psi_{\mathbf n},\psi_{\mathbf m}\rangle_{L^2}=\delta_{\mathbf n\mathbf m},\qquad \overline{\operatorname{span}}\{\psi_{\mathbf n}\}=L^2(\mathbb R^N),$$
and
$$\left(-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2+c|q|^2\right)\psi_{\mathbf n} =\epsilon_{\mathbf n}\psi_{\mathbf n},\qquad \epsilon_{\mathbf n}:=\sum_{j=1}^N(2n_j+1)\sqrt{a_jc}.$$
For the ground multi-index $\mathbf0$, the smooth representative is
$$\psi_{\mathbf0}(q)=\prod_{j=1}^N(b_j/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-b_jq_j^2/2}, \qquad b_j:=\sqrt{c/a_j}.$$
Each $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ belongs to $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and every $u\in
Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ satisfies the exact form expansion
$$\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+ c\||q|u\|_2^2 =\sum_{\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^N}\epsilon_{\mathbf n} |\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2.$$
All parameters are positive real mathematical parameters; this lemma makes no
physical identification.

Assume Countable Choice and use $Q$, $q_h$, and the operator $h$ from
[[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]]. Let $\lambda_1$ be the least
eigenvalue of $h$. Then
$$\inf\{q_h(u):u\in Q,\ \|u\|_2=1\}=\lambda_1.$$
The infimum is attained by every normalized vector in the lowest eigenspace;
no simplicity or nondegeneracy is assumed.

Assume Countable Choice. Use the finite data and notation of
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]: $N\ge1$,
$H_N=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, $D_0=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
and $W=V+C_0+1\ge1+c|q|^2$. For $u,v\in D_0$ define
$$a(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int_{\mathbb R^N}(\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv}\,dq+\int_{\mathbb R^N}(W+1)u\overline v\,dq,$$
and $\|u\|_Q:=a(u,u)^{1/2}$. Let $Q$ be the completion of this inner-product
space, constructed as equivalence classes of $\|\cdot\|_Q$-Cauchy sequences.
Then $Q$ is a complex Hilbert space and the map sending a Cauchy class to its
$L^2$ limit is a continuous injective linear map $Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ with
dense image. Each $u\in Q$ has weak derivatives $\partial_j u\in L^2$ and a
weighted function $\sqrt{W+1}\,u\in L^2$, and
$$\|u\|_Q^2=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2.$$
Here $g_j=\partial_j u$ means explicitly that
$\int u\,\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$ for every
$\varphi\in D_0$.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Write $a_\lambda=q_\lambda+2\|\cdot\|_2^2$ for the shifted form inner product of the $\lambda$ completion. On $C_c^\infty$, $V_\lambda\ge V_0$ gives $a_\lambda(u,u)\ge a_0(u,u)$, so a $Q_\lambda$-Cauchy sequence is $Q_0$-Cauchy and the identity extends continuously to $Q_\lambda\to Q_0$ with the same $L^2$ representative. The unshifted forms $q_\lambda=a_\lambda-2\|\cdot\|_2^2$ and $q_0=a_0-2\|\cdot\|_2^2$ are continuous on their respective form spaces. For any $u\in Q_\lambda$, approximate it in $Q_\lambda$ by $u_r\in C_c^\infty$; then $q_\lambda(u_r)\ge q_0(u_r)$ for every $r$, and continuity of both forms gives $q_\lambda(u)\ge q_0(u)$ in the limit. For normalized $u\in Q_\lambda$, [F3] then gives $q_\lambda(u)\ge q_0(u)\ge E_g(0)$. Taking the infimum yields $E_g(\lambda)\ge E_g(0)$.

The Gaussian $\phi_b$ from [F2] and its derivative are polynomial times a Gaussian. For cutoffs $\chi_R$ as in the cutoff construction of
[[lem-qft-hermite-oscillator-research-supplier]], $\chi_R\phi_b\in C_c^\infty$
converges to $\phi_b$ in the $\lambda$ form norm: the derivative error is
$(1-\chi_R)\phi_b'-(\chi_R')\phi_b$, whose first term has vanishing Gaussian
tail and whose second has norm at most $C\|\phi_b\|_2/R$; the weighted error
has squared magnitude bounded by $(m^2q^2/2+\lambda q^4+2)|\phi_b|^2$, an
integrable polynomial-Gaussian tail. Thus $\phi_b\in Q_\lambda$.

Let $\mathbb E_b[g]:=\int g(q)\sqrt{b/\pi}e^{-bq^2}\,dq$. The Hermite
ground function in [F2] is normalized, so $\mathbb E_b[1]=1$. On any compact
interval of positive $b$ values, the derivatives of the integrands through
order two are bounded by a constant times $(1+|q|^4)e^{-b_*q^2}$ for some
$b_*>0$, which is integrable; [F5] therefore permits differentiation under the
integral. Differentiating $\mathbb E_b[1]=1$ gives
$$0=\mathbb E_b\!\left[\frac1{2b}-q^2\right],\qquad \mathbb E_b[q^2]=\frac1{2b}.$$
Differentiating the second identity and using
$\partial_b(\sqrt{b/\pi}e^{-bq^2})=(\frac1{2b}-q^2)\sqrt{b/\pi}e^{-bq^2}$ gives
$$-\frac1{2b^2}=\mathbb E_b\!\left[q^2\left(\frac1{2b}-q^2\right)\right] =\frac1{4b^2}-\mathbb E_b[q^4],$$
so $\mathbb E_b[q^4]=3/(4b^2)$. Since $\phi_b'=-bq\phi_b$, this gives
$\|\phi_b'\|_2^2=b/2$. Hence
$$\|\phi_b\|_2^2=1,\quad \|\phi_b'\|_2^2=b/2,\quad \int q^2|\phi_b|^2=1/(2b),\quad\int q^4|\phi_b|^2=3/(4b^2).$$
The unperturbed form value
is $ab/2+m^2/(4b)=m\sqrt{a/2}=E_g(0)$, using $b=m/\sqrt{2a}$, and the quartic
contribution is $3\lambda/(4b^2)=3a\lambda/(2m^2)$. The variational bound
[F3] applied to this normalized vector yields
$$E_g(\lambda)\le E_g(0)+\frac{3a\lambda}{2m^2}.$$
Combining with step 1.1 proves both inequalities, including $\lambda=0$.

Their difference is $|n\rangle$; linear extension proves $[a(e),a^\dagger(e)]=I$ on the finite-particle core. For fermions, $c(e)\Omega=0$, $c^\dagger(e)\Omega=|1\rangle$, $c(e)|1\rangle=\Omega$, and $c^\dagger(e)|1\rangle=0$. Hence $\{c(e),c^\dagger(e)\}$ fixes both basis vectors, while $c(e)^2=(c^\dagger(e))^2=0$; these identities hold on the whole two-dimensional fermionic Fock space.

The squared norm of $\Psi$ is $\sum_{n\ge0}(n+1)^{-3}$, which is finite: on each block $2^k\le n+1<2^{k+1}$ there are $2^k$ terms, each at most $2^{-3k}$, so the block sum is at most $2^{-2k}$ and the geometric series of these bounds converges. By [F3], $\Psi\in D(N)$ would require $\sum_{n\ge1}n^2/(n+1)^3<\infty$. Since $n+1\le2n$ for $n\ge1$, $n^2/(n+1)^3\ge1/(8n)$. The harmonic series diverges because each block $2^k\le n<2^{k+1}$ has $2^k$ terms at least $2^{-(k+1)}$, so every block sum is at least $1/2$. Therefore $\Psi\notin D(N)$.

By [F2], the annihilation-domain sum for $\Psi$ is $\sum_{n\ge1}n/(n+1)^3\le\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-2}$, and the creation-domain sum is $\sum_{n\ge0}(n+1)^{-2}$. Each is finite: the $k$th dyadic block of $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-2}$ has at most $2^k$ terms each at most $2^{-2k}$, so its block sum is at most $2^{-k}$; the shifted series has the same convergence. Thus $\Psi\in D(a(e))\cap D(a^\dagger(e))$ while step 1.2 proves $\Psi\notin D(N)$. This is a domain distinction for the stated operators, not a physical or empirical claim.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $j=(j_1,j_2,j_3)\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R^3)$ and use $\mathcal H_T$ and $P_T$ from [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]]. For $\omega=|\mathbf k|$ and $\mathbf k\ne0$, define
$$g_j(\mathbf k)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3/2}(2\omega)^{1/2}}\, P_T(\mathbf k)\int_{\mathbb R^4}j(x)e^{i\omega x^0-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\,d^4x.$$
Then $g_j\in\mathcal H_T$. On the finite-particle domain $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ of the bosonic Fock space $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$, the smeared transverse potential is
$$A_T(j)=a(g_j)+a^\dagger(g_j).$$
Its matrix elements are continuous in the test-function topology; it is an operator-valued distribution and does not assign a pointwise operator to $A_i(x)$. With $E_i=-\partial_0A_i$, the equal-time canonical commutator is the distribution
$$[A_i(0,\mathbf x),E_j(0,\mathbf y)] =-i\,P_{T,ij}(-i\nabla_{\mathbf x})\delta^3(\mathbf x-\mathbf y).$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $G(\mathbf x)=1/(4\pi|\mathbf x|)$ on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, interpreted as its locally integrable distribution, and use the Fourier convention
$$\widehat f(\mathbf k)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}f(\mathbf x)\,d^3\mathbf x,\qquad f(\mathbf x)=(2\pi)^{-3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\widehat f(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k.$$
Then $\mathcal F^{-1}(|\mathbf k|^{-2})=G$ distributionally. Consequently, for $P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)=\delta_{ij}-k_i k_j/|\mathbf k|^2$,
$$P_{T,ij}(-i\nabla)\delta^3 =\delta_{ij}\delta^3+\partial_i\partial_jG.$$
For $\mathbf x\ne0$,
$$\partial_i\partial_jG(\mathbf x) =-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{4\pi|\mathbf x|^3} +\frac{3x_ix_j}{4\pi|\mathbf x|^5}.$$
Thus the equal-time transverse-potential commutator of [[lem-qft-photon-smeared-potential]] has this off-diagonal Newtonian kernel (with its stated factor $-i$). The identity is distributional at the origin; the displayed classical derivative formula is only asserted away from it.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Choose nonnegative smooth tests $f,g$ from [F3], supported in small disjoint balls centered at points whose difference is $z_0$, with the difference of their supports contained in that neighborhood. $$\mathcal K_0=\{\epsilon\in\mathcal K:-\epsilon^0+n\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon=0\text{ a.e.}\},\qquad T\epsilon=\boldsymbol\epsilon-n\epsilon^0.$$
Then $\mathcal K_0$ is closed, $T:\mathcal K_0\to\mathcal H_T$ is bounded and onto, and
$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\langle T\epsilon,T\delta\rangle_2\quad(\epsilon,\delta\in\mathcal K_0).$$
Its radical (the vectors pairing to zero with all of $\mathcal K_0$) is
$$\mathcal N=\ker T=\{b(\mathbf k)(1,n(\mathbf k)):b\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)\}.$$
Consequently $\mathcal K_0/\mathcal N$ with the induced form is a positive Hilbert space isometric to $\mathcal H_T$. The form on the four-component auxiliary space is indefinite; only the subsidiary quotient is the positive physical one-particle space.

Assume Countable Choice. For $n\in S^2\subset\mathbb R^3$, let $E_n=n^\perp=\operatorname{Ran}(I-nn^T)$ be the real transverse plane. There do not exist continuous maps $e_1,e_2:S^2\to\mathbb R^3$ such that, for every $n$, $(e_1(n),e_2(n))$ is an orthonormal basis of $E_n$. A continuous real orthonormal polarization frame would in particular give a continuous nowhere-zero tangent vector field on $S^2$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

For $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$, $\|u\times v\|_2^2=\det G(u,v)$, and this value is positive exactly when $u$ and $v$ are linearly independent.

Equivalently,
$$\|u\times v\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2\|v\|_2^2-\langle u,v\rangle^2.$$

derivations.claim: Since $n$ is unit, $P_T(n)=I-nn^T$ has kernel $\mathbb R n$ and range $n^\perp$, of dimension $3-1=2$, by [F1]. For any fixed unit vector $u$ not parallel to $n_0$, $P_T(n)u$ is nonzero on a neighborhood of $n_0$; there define $e_1(n)=P_T(n)u/|P_T(n)u|$ and $e_2(n)=n\times e_1(n)$. By [F4], $e_2$ is orthogonal to both unit vectors and $|e_2|^2=1-0=1$. It is therefore a continuous unit vector in $n^\perp$, orthogonal to $e_1$, so the two vectors form a local frame.

The quotient in [F2] is positive and isometric to the range in step 1.1, so it has exactly two physical directions in each nonzero momentum fiber. A global continuous real frame would contradict [F3]. Thus the local construction cannot be made into a single continuous frame over the whole sphere.

citations.quote:
Use the transverse one-particle space $\mathcal H_T$ and multiplier $\omega(\mathbf k)$ of [[def-qft-qed-photon-energy-multiplier]], and form its symmetric Fock space $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$. Let $H_{\rm ph}:=\hbar c\,d\Gamma(\omega)$, with $\hbar,c>0$ and $d\Gamma(\omega)$ acting on the $n$-particle sector as multiplication by $\sum_{j=1}^n|\mathbf k_j|$, as in [[lem-qft-second-quantized-spectrum]]. For a coherent vector use
$$ \epsilon(f):=\bigoplus_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{f^{\otimes n}}{\sqrt{n!}},\qquad C(f):=e^{-\|f\|^2/2}\epsilon(f), $$
using the tensor and direct-sum conventions of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]].

Let $\kappa>0$. Let $b:S^2\to\mathbb C^3$ be measurable with $b\in L^2(S^2,d\Omega;\mathbb C^3)$, $\mathbf n\cdot b(\mathbf n)=0$ for a.e. $\mathbf n$, and
$$ C_b:=\int_{S^2}|b(\mathbf n)|^2\,d\Omega>0. $$
Take $\mathbf k,\kappa,\epsilon$ in inverse metres and $b$ dimensionless; then $f_\epsilon$ has momentum-wavefunction units $\mathrm m^{3/2}$, $C_b$ is dimensionless, and $\hbar c(\kappa-\epsilon)$ has energy units.
For $0<\epsilon<\kappa$, define $f_\epsilon(0)=0$ and
$$ f_\epsilon(\mathbf k):=\mathbf1_{\{\epsilon<|\mathbf k|<\kappa\}}|\mathbf k|^{-3/2}b\!\left(\frac{\mathbf k}{|\mathbf k|}\right). $$
Then
$$ \|f_\epsilon\|^2=C_b\log\frac{\kappa}{\epsilon},\qquad \langle C(f_\epsilon),H_{\rm ph}C(f_\epsilon)\rangle =\hbar c\,C_b(\kappa-\epsilon). $$
Each $C(f_\epsilon)$ is a unit vector in $D(H_{\rm ph})$. As $\epsilon\downarrow0$, $C(f_\epsilon)\rightharpoonup0$ weakly, but the family has no strong Fock-space limit. The statement is an exact free transverse-mode construction; it asserts no interacting charged sector, continuum QED limit, or empirical observation.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and $n\ge2$. The chart surface measure on $S^{n-1}$ equals the polar measure $\sigma$. Orthogonal transformations preserve it. The map $\omega\mapsto a+R\omega$, $R>0$, multiplies surface measure by $R^{n-1}$, and $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For $b(n)=P_T(n)e$, $|b(n)|^2=1-(n\cdot e)^2$. By [F2], rotate $e$ to the third coordinate axis. The regular sphere chart $X(y,z)=(\sqrt{1-y^2-z^2},y,z)$ on $|y|,|z|<1/4$ lies in the belt $|n\cdot e|<1/2$ and has area density $(1-y^2-z^2)^{-1/2}\ge1$ by [F3]. Its parameter rectangle has area $1/4$, so this belt has positive surface measure. On the belt $|b(n)|^2\ge3/4$, hence $C_b>0$; also $b$ is continuous, square-integrable on the finite sphere measure, and transverse.

Apply [F1] to this $b$. It gives unit vectors with $0\le\langle C(f_\epsilon),H_{\rm ph}C(f_\epsilon)\rangle\le\hbar c\,C_b\kappa<\infty$, yet no strong Fock-space limit. This contradicts the asserted implication and is the required counterexample.

citations.quote: every physical vector has total occupation

derivations.claim: Here $G_{v_1}=E_e-n_{v_1}$ and $G_{v_2}=-E_e-n_{v_2}$, so $G_{v_1}+G_{v_2}=-(n_{v_1}+n_{v_2})$ on their common domain; the link flux cancels.

The zero-background identity from [F1] requires $n_{v_1}+n_{v_2}=0$ on every physical vector. The normalized occupation vector with $n_{v_1}=1,n_{v_2}=0$ has total number one, so it is not physical and the asserted every-sector property fails.
